channel.title: Words with Stories — On Life & Everything
channel.description: A small collection of words whose older meaning still shows through the modern one. Every story sourced.

item.title: freelance
item.description: Freelance began as a name for a hired medieval warrior in nineteenth-century writing. The lance belonged to someone who could choose whom to serve.
item.content:encoded:
A freelance worker takes on work without a lasting commitment to one employer. The word first named a hired warrior. The lance was a weapon, and its bearer could offer his service to whoever would pay. 1

The word appeared in the early nineteenth century. Merriam-Webster’s earliest written evidence comes from Walter Scott’s Ivanhoe, where a lord speaks of his “Free Lances” after offering their services to Richard. Scott was writing about medieval life long after the period itself. 1

The expression widened to include politicians who belonged to no party and people who worked independently. By the late nineteenth century it was being applied to journalism. The modern adjective keeps the idea of offering a skill without committing to a single employer. 12

She works as a freelance editor.

Sources

  1. The Surprising History of ‘Freelance’ — Merriam-Webster
  2. Freelance — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: prestige
item.description: Prestige once meant a trick or illusion. In the nineteenth century it developed the favourable sense of reputation and standing.
item.content:encoded:
Prestige is the standing someone has in other people’s eyes. When English borrowed the word from French in the seventeenth century, it meant a trick or illusion. Its Latin ancestry belongs to conjuring and deception. 12

In the nineteenth century the word began to describe the impressive appearance of someone’s importance or ability. It could still suggest a flattering illusion, but it also came to mean the reputation itself. Admiration became part of the word’s ordinary meaning. 1

Prestigious had entered English separately, from a related Latin word meaning deceitful or full of tricks. It kept that sense for centuries before acquiring its familiar meaning of highly regarded around the beginning of the twentieth century. Both words had moved from deception to esteem.2

The discovery brought considerable prestige to the university.

Sources

  1. Prestige — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. The Original Meaning of ‘Prestigious’ — Merriam-Webster

item.title: villain
item.description: Villain comes from a word for a villager or farm worker. Contempt for someone’s social rank became a judgement about their character.
item.content:encoded:
The villain in a story has a name that once belonged to a villager. The word comes through French from Medieval Latin villanus, a rural inhabitant or farm worker, derived from villa.12

In medieval usage, the name carried the contempt of people who ranked themselves above those who worked the land. A person of low birth was assumed to have coarse manners. The judgement then extended to morals: someone considered uncouth became someone considered wicked. 1

By the sixteenth century villain could mean a scoundrel. The familiar use for a character whose evil actions drive a play or novel came later. The spelling villein kept the historical sense of a peasant bound to a lord’s land, while villain became the usual form of the insult. 2

The villain was the most interesting character in the play.

Sources

  1. The History of the Word ‘Villain’ — Merriam-Webster
  2. Villain — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: awful
item.description: Awful once described something that inspired awe, fear or reverence. The same word now serves for an unpleasant meal or a bad day.
item.content:encoded:
Awful carries awe inside it. In its older uses, something awful inspired fear or reverence. The word could describe the power of something that made people feel small or deeply respectful.1

That strength gradually weakened in everyday use. By around the beginning of the nineteenth century, awful was being used for things that were very bad or disagreeable. It also became an intensifier: an awful lot is a great quantity. A word suited to dread could now describe a disappointing meal.12

The older meaning remains available, especially in literary writing. Merriam-Webster gives George Eliot’s phrase “awful loveliness” as an example. There the beauty inspires awe. Reading it as a complaint would change the sense of the passage.2

The weather was awful, so we stayed inside.

Sources

  1. Awful — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Awful — Merriam-Webster

item.title: silly
item.description: Silly descends from an Old English word for happiness and good fortune. Its history passes through innocence and helplessness on the way to foolishness.
item.content:encoded:
Silly began with good fortune. Its Old English ancestor meant happy or fortunate, and the related German word selig still means blessed or blissful. In Middle English, forms such as sely and seely carried meanings including blessed and innocent. 12

Innocence could also suggest being harmless or unable to defend oneself. The word came to describe someone deserving pity, then someone weak. By the sixteenth century it could describe a person judged to lack sense. These meanings developed along overlapping paths, with innocence and helplessness giving way to foolishness.1

Today silly can be a mild criticism of someone’s judgement or an affectionate word for playful behaviour. The older meanings survive in texts where a “silly” person may be helpless or humble.2

I made a silly mistake when I copied the address.

Sources

  1. Silly — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Silly — Merriam-Webster

item.title: nice
item.description: Nice once meant foolish or ignorant. Its later meanings included fussy, delicate and precise before it became an everyday word of approval.
item.content:encoded:
Calling someone nice is usually a compliment. When the word reached English from French in the late thirteenth century, it could mean foolish or ignorant. Behind it was Latin nescius, meaning unaware or not knowing.1

The change took centuries. Among its later meanings were fussy and hard to please, then delicate and precise. Something nice could require careful attention or a discriminating taste. By the eighteenth century the word was also being used for things that pleased, and later for people who were kind or considerate.1

Some of those meanings still coexist. A nice distinction is a subtle or precise distinction; someone with a nice palate is particular about what they taste. These uses preserve the exacting sense alongside the much broader approval in a nice day.2

It was nice of her to wait for us.

Sources

  1. Nice — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Nice — Merriam-Webster

item.title: sherbet
item.description: Sherbet is the Turkish şerbet, a drink, from an Arabic word for a draught. Syrup came from the same Arabic root by an older road, and sorbet by a later one.
item.content:encoded:
Sherbet is now a frozen dessert or, in Britain, a fizzy sweet powder. The word is the Turkish şerbet, a drink, from Persian sharbat and Arabic sharba, from the verb shariba, to drink.1

In Arabic, sharba was a single draught, the amount drunk at one time.2

English met the drink in the 1580s and spelled it many ways, among them sorbet, zerbet and cherbet.1

The same Arabic root had reached English long before, by another road. Syrup came in the late fourteenth century through Old French sirop, from Arabic sharāb, a drink or wine.1

The frozen sense arrived through Italian sorbetto in the eighteenth century, and in the nineteenth English took the French sorbet for it again.1

They drank cold sherbet in the shade.

Sources

  1. Sherbet — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Şerbet — Nişanyan Sözlük

item.title: checkmate
item.description: Checkmate comes through French and Arabic from the Persian shāh, king. The same king gave English check, the Exchequer and, probably by way of it, the spelling cheque.
item.content:encoded:
Checkmate ends a game of chess: the king is attacked and cannot escape. The word came into English in the fourteenth century from Old French eschec mat, from Arabic shāh māt.1

The Arabic is usually read as “the king died.” But shāh is the Persian word for king, and Persian māt can mean astonished, so the phrase may first have meant that the king was left helpless rather than dead.1

Check comes from the same shāh, and it travelled far from the board. The officials of the Norman kings of England counted the royal revenue with counters on a table covered with a chequered cloth, which looked like a chessboard, and their department became the Exchequer.2 The bank cheque, from 1798, probably took its spelling from the exchequer.1

Three moves later it was checkmate.

Sources

  1. Checkmate — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Exchequer — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: chauvinism
item.description: Chauvinism is named after Nicolas Chauvin, a soldier devoted to Napoleon who is known from an 1831 play. Whether a real Chauvin stood behind him has never been settled.
item.content:encoded:
Chauvinism is a blind belief that one’s own group is better than others. The word is French, chauvinisme, and it is named after Nicolas Chauvin, a soldier who stayed devoted to Napoleon long after the Empire had ended.12

Chauvin is known as a character. He appears in La Cocarde tricolore, a popular comic play by the brothers Théodore and Hippolyte Cogniard, staged in 1831.12

Whether a real Chauvin stood behind him has never been settled. The name was common in Napoleon’s army, and an 1822 memoir mentions a Chauvin who came back with Napoleon from Elba, but no one has shown that he was the man.1

English took chauvinism in 1840 for excessive patriotism. Male chauvinist was in use by 1936 and became common after 1969.1

The speech was full of national chauvinism.

Sources

  1. Chauvinism — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Chauvinism — Merriam-Webster

item.title: tragedy
item.description: Tragedy is the Greek tragōidia, a goat song. Why a goat is not known. The word went from a kind of play to any calamity.
item.content:encoded:
A tragedy is a terrible event, and before that it was a kind of play with a sorrowful end. The Greek tragōidia is made of tragos, a goat, and ōidē, a song.1

Why a goat is not known. One explanation looks to satyr plays, whose performers wore goatskins. Another looks to a singer who competed for a goat as a prize. Some doubt the goat altogether.1 Aristotle wrote that tragedy began with the authors of the dithyramb and grew away from the grotesque manner of the satyric form.2

English took the word in the late fourteenth century for a serious story that ends in misery. Chaucer, translating Boethius, defined it as prosperity that ends in wretchedness. By about 1500 a tragedy could be any calamity.1

The fire was a tragedy for the whole street.

Sources

  1. Tragedy — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Poetics, Part IV — Aristotle, translated by S. H. Butcher, The Internet Classics Archive

item.title: hazard
item.description: Hazard was first a game of dice. It may go back to an Arabic word for a die, though that origin is doubted, and in English it came to mean a risk of harm.
item.content:encoded:
A hazard is a danger, a risk that something will go wrong. In English it was first the name of a game of dice, around 1300. The French hasard meant the game and also a throw of six.12

The word may have come into French from Arabic. Merriam-Webster traces it through Spanish azar to Arabic az-zahr, the die, probably borrowed during the Crusades.2

That origin is doubted. The Online Etymology Dictionary notes that zahr does not appear in the classical Arabic dictionaries, and records Ernest Klein’s suggestion of yasara, he played at dice, instead.1

The meaning moved from the throw to the chances of life. Since the 1540s a hazard in English has been a risk of loss or harm.1

The ice on the steps is a hazard.

Sources

  1. Hazard — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Hazard — Merriam-Webster

item.title: bergamot
item.description: Bergamot first named a pear, traced to the Turkish bey armudu, the bey’s pear. Dictionaries disagree whether the citrus took that name or the name of the Italian town of Bergamo.
item.content:encoded:
Bergamot is a small citrus fruit with a fragrant, bitter oil in its rind.1 Where its name comes from is not settled.

The word first named a pear. In the 1610s English used bergamot for an especially fine pear, and the Online Etymology Dictionary traces that name to the Turkish bey armudu, the bey’s pear, reshaped in Italian to sound like the town of Bergamo.2

For the citrus, which came into English in the 1690s, the same dictionary takes the town itself: Bergamo, in northern Italy.2 Merriam-Webster gives the citrus the Turkish pear instead.1

Both dictionaries find the Turkish pear in the word. They disagree about whether the citrus owes its name to the pear or to the town.

The tea smelled of bergamot.

Sources

  1. Bergamot — Merriam-Webster
  2. Bergamot — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: mercurial
item.description: Mercurial first meant of the planet Mercury. Astrology gave those born under it the messenger god’s quickness, and the liquid metal probably helped the word mean changeable.
item.content:encoded:
A mercurial person changes mood quickly and without warning. In the late fourteenth century the word meant “of the planet Mercury,” from Latin Mercurialis.12

Mercury was also the Roman messenger god, quick and clever, and astrology gave his qualities to those born under his planet. By the 1640s English used mercurial for a lively, quick and changeable temperament.1

The metal probably helped. Mercury, or quicksilver, stays liquid and runs at a touch, and medicine still calls anything containing it mercurial.12

His mercurial temper kept everyone guessing.

Sources

  1. Mercurial — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Mercurial — Merriam-Webster

item.title: jovial
item.description: Jovial means of Jove, another name for Jupiter. Astrology held that people born under the planet Jupiter were cheerful, and the word kept the cheer.
item.content:encoded:
A jovial person is cheerful and good company. The word means “of Jove,” another name for Jupiter, the chief Roman god. It reached English from French in the 1580s with an astrological sense: under the influence of the planet Jupiter.1

Astrology held that people shared the nature of the planet that ruled their birth. Those born under Jupiter were thought to be cheerful, and the word kept the cheer after the belief had gone.12

It was often set against saturnine, gloomy. In Roman myth Saturn was Jupiter’s father.2

Our jovial host kept everyone’s glass full.

Sources

  1. Jovial — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Jovial — Merriam-Webster

item.title: saturnine
item.description: Saturnine means gloomy because astrology held that people born under Saturn shared its coldness and slowness. Saturn was also the alchemists’ name for lead.
item.content:encoded:
A saturnine person is gloomy and slow to warm. The word means “of Saturn,” and in the fifteenth century it described someone born under that planet’s influence.12

Saturn was thought to be the planet farthest from the Sun, and so the coldest and the slowest. Old medicine held that people born under it took on its nature.1

Renaissance writers gave the planet a second side. Marsilio Ficino, himself born under Saturn, tied it to melancholy and to the deep thought of scholars, so that a child of Saturn could be gloomy and gifted at once.3

Saturn was also the alchemists’ name for lead, so saturnine can mean “of lead.” Medicine still uses it that way: saturnine gout is caused by lead poisoning.12

He gave a saturnine smile and said nothing.

Sources

  1. Saturnine — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Saturnine — Merriam-Webster
  3. The Secret Life of Saturn: Melancholia and the Warburg Institute — The Marginalia Review of Books

item.title: divan
item.description: Divan began as a Persian word for written sheets. It became an office, a council, the seat along the council chamber’s walls and a poet’s collected poems.
item.content:encoded:
A divan is a low sofa, usually without a back. The word began in Persian, where devan meant a bundle of written sheets or a small book.1

In Arabic, dīwān moved from a book of accounts to the office that kept them, and from there to a government office and the council that met in its chamber.12 English first took the word from Turkish in the 1580s, for a council of state.1

The seat came from the room. The long cushioned benches along the walls of a council chamber were called divans, and English has used the word for a sofa since 1702.1

Two other senses went their own way. A divan is also a poet’s collected poems, as in the Divan of Hafez.12 In Italy the Arabic word became dogana, earlier doana, the customs house.3

He fell asleep on the divan with the book still open.

Sources

  1. Divan — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Dīvān — Encyclopædia Iranica
  3. Dogana — Vocabolario Treccani

item.title: thrill
item.description: A thrill once pierced. The Old English þyrlian, to pierce, came from þyrel, a hole, the same hole that is still in nostril.
item.content:encoded:
A thrill is a sudden rush of excitement or fear that seems to go right through you. The word began with exactly that. The Old English verb þyrlian meant to pierce, and it came from þyrel, a hole. In Middle English thirlen became thrillen, as two of its sounds changed places.1

By the late fourteenth century the verb could be used of a feeling that pierces someone. The shivering, exciting feeling is recorded from the 1590s, and the noun from the 1670s.1

The same hole is still in nostril. Old English nosþyrl was the hole of the nose, from nosu, nose, and þyrel.2

A thrill went through the crowd when the doors opened.

Sources

  1. Thrill — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Nostril — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: calculate
item.description: Calculate comes from the Latin calculus, a small pebble used as a counter. The stone is still there in a doctor’s calculus and in calcium.
item.content:encoded:
To calculate is to work something out with numbers. The Latin calculare meant to reckon, and it was built on calculus, a small pebble, from calx, limestone.1

The pebbles were counters. On a Roman counting board they were moved along grooves to hold the figures of a sum.12

English took calculate in the 1560s. A century later calculus became the name of a method in mathematics.1

Medicine kept the stone. Since the early eighteenth century a calculus has been a stone formed in the body, such as a kidney stone, and dentists use the word for hardened plaque.1

The limestone kept its name too. When Humphry Davy isolated a new metal in 1808, he called it calcium, after calx.3

She calculated how long the journey would take.

Sources

  1. Calculate — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Abacus — Encyclopædia Britannica
  3. Calcium — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: clue
item.description: A clue was a ball of thread. The thread Ariadne gave Theseus, which led him out of the Labyrinth, turned the word into anything that shows the way.
item.content:encoded:
A clue is something that helps you find an answer. It was once a clew, a ball of thread or yarn, from the Old English cliewen, a ball or skein.1

The change came from a Greek myth. Ariadne gave Theseus a thread to take into the Labyrinth, and once he had killed the Minotaur he followed it back out. Ovid tells the story in the Metamorphoses.2

From the 1590s English used the word for anything that guides a person through an intricate case, and by the 1620s for whatever points the way, with no labyrinth involved.1

The spelling changed as well. Middle English often wrote French words ending in -ue with -ew, and when their spelling went back to -ue, some native words followed, among them hue, true and clue. The spelling clue appears in the middle of the fifteenth century, and clew survived for the thread in northern English and Scots.1

There was no clue to who had written the letter.

Sources

  1. Clue — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Metamorphoses, Book VIII — Ovid, translated by A. S. Kline, Poetry in Translation

item.title: meander
item.description: Meander is the name of a river in western Türkiye, the Maeander, now the Büyük Menderes. Its course was so winding that its name came to mean any winding course.
item.content:encoded:
To meander is to wind slowly, as a river does, or a person with nowhere in particular to be. The word is the name of a river: Greek Maiandros, Latin Maeander.1

The river still runs. It is the Büyük Menderes, the longest river in western Türkiye, which once divided the ancient regions of Caria and Lydia.2

It was known for its bends. Strabo, writing about two thousand years ago, said its course was so winding that everything winding was called after it.3 Greeks already used the river’s name for winding patterns.1

English took the noun in the 1570s, first for an intricate confusion and from the 1590s for the bends of a river. The verb followed in the 1610s for a river’s winding flow, and by the 1830s a person could meander too.1

We meandered along the shore with no plan.

Sources

  1. Meander — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Meander (Büyük Menderes) — Livius
  3. Geography, Book XII, Chapter 8 — Strabo, translated by H. L. Jones, LacusCurtius

item.title: ballot
item.description: Ballot comes from an Italian word for a small ball used in voting. The name survived when votes were recorded on paper.
item.content:encoded:
A ballot is a vote, or the paper on which someone records one. The word once referred to a small ball.12

Italian ballotta meant a little ball. In Venice, small balls could be used to register votes without a public show of hands. English borrowed the word for this way of voting.12

Paper ballots eventually took the place of the little balls, and the name went with them. The object changed, while the word kept its place in an election.1

The voters marked their ballots in private.

Sources

  1. Ballot — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Ballot — Oxford Advanced Learner’s Dictionary

item.title: parliament
item.description: Parliament grew from an Old French word for speaking and discussion. The institution kept the name as assemblies changed.
item.content:encoded:
A parliament is an assembly that debates and makes laws. Before it named an institution, the word named a conversation.1

Old French parlement meant a speaking or discussion, from parler, to speak. English borrowed the word for formal gatherings in the Middle Ages. It came to mean an assembly summoned by a ruler.12

The English Parliament grew out of the great councils at which the king met the leading men of the kingdom. Knights from the counties had sometimes been summoned before, and in 1265 the towns were also asked to send burgesses. It gradually became established that people outside the aristocracy would be summoned.2

Parliament met again after the recess.

Sources

  1. Parliament — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. List of people summoned to the 1265 Parliament — The National Archives

item.title: placebo
item.description: Placebo means I shall please in Latin. It named a prayer service, then flattery, before becoming a term in medicine.
item.content:encoded:
A placebo can be an inactive preparation given in a medical study. The word once belonged to a prayer.1

In Latin, placebo means I shall please. It began a verse sung in the evening service for the dead, and the service came to be called by that first word.12

In medieval English, to sing placebo could mean to flatter someone. By the eighteenth century, physicians used the word for something given to please a patient rather than for a specific therapeutic action.12

Placebos later became important in controlled studies, where they help researchers distinguish the effects of a treatment from effects associated with receiving care and expecting improvement. A word from the service for the dead became part of the language of testing medicine.1

Half the volunteers received a placebo.

Sources

  1. Placebo — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. Placebo — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: anatomy
item.description: Anatomy is Greek for a cutting up. The same root is in atom, what cannot be cut, and anatomy misheard once gave English atomy, a skeleton.
item.content:encoded:
Anatomy is the study of the structure of the body. The Greek anatomē, from which it comes, meant dissection, literally a cutting up.1

The same Greek root for cutting is in atom. Greek atomos meant indivisible, that which cannot be cut. Anatomy names the cutting of a body into its parts; an atom was named as something that could not be cut at all.12

In older English, an anatomy was also heard as an atomy, and atomy became a word of its own for a skeleton, or for a person thin enough to look like one.3

Anatomy can now mean the body’s structure itself, and it can be used for the detailed examination of other things.1

The students studied the anatomy of the hand.

Sources

  1. Anatomy — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. Atom — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  3. Atomy — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language

item.title: focus
item.description: Focus is the Latin word for a hearth. Kepler gave it to mathematics in 1604, probably after the point where a lens or a mirror gathers sunlight hot enough to start a fire.
item.content:encoded:
A focus is a point where light rays meet, or a place at which we direct our attention. In Latin, focus meant a hearth.12

Johannes Kepler gave the word to mathematics in 1604, in a book on the optical part of astronomy. He used it for the two points of an ellipse that are still called its foci.3

The reason for a hearth is given as probable rather than certain. A lens or a curved mirror can gather sunlight onto one point and start a fire there.12

From the point where rays meet, the word reached photography and ordinary speech. We can focus a camera, and we can focus our minds.12

She adjusted the focus until the lettering was clear.

Sources

  1. Focus — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. Focus — Online Etymology Dictionary
  3. Earliest Known Uses of Some of the Words of Mathematics (F) — Jeff Miller, MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews

item.title: wow
item.description: Wow appears in early Scots writing. In 1977, Jerry Ehman’s handwritten reaction to an unusual radio signal gave the Wow! signal its name.
item.content:encoded:
Wow can sound very modern. The Dictionaries of the Scots Language records it in Peblis to the Play, with the example dated before 1500, and in Gavin Douglas’s writing of 1513.1

Those early examples carry astonishment and fear as well as admiration. In one from 1540, someone cries out at what they see. In another, a frightened speaker asks for room to get away.1

By 1924, American slang also used wow as a verb, for overwhelming someone with delight, the sense in which a performer wows an audience.2

In 1977, the exclamation acquired a place in astronomy. On August 15, Ohio State University’s Big Ear radio telescope detected an unusually strong radio signal during a search for extraterrestrial intelligence. A few days later, the volunteer astronomer Jerry Ehman was reviewing the computer printout when he noticed the sequence 6EQUJ5. He marked the characters in red and wrote “Wow!” in the margin. His colleague John Kraus began calling it the Wow! signal.3

The six characters showed the signal growing stronger and then fading as the Earth’s rotation carried the telescope’s view past that part of the sky, which is what a compact radio source in the sky would do.34 Follow-up observations have not detected the same signal again, and its origin remains unresolved.34

Wow, I hadn’t realized how high we had climbed.

Sources

  1. Wow, interj. — Dictionaries of the Scots Language
  2. Wow — Online Etymology Dictionary
  3. The Big Ear Wow! Signal, 30th Anniversary Report — Jerry R. Ehman, Ohio State University Radio Observatory
  4. The Wow Signal — SETI Institute

item.title: cobalt
item.description: Cobalt takes its name from the German Kobold, a goblin blamed by miners when troublesome ores failed to yield the silver they expected.
item.content:encoded:
The metal behind cobalt blue takes its name from a goblin. German miners used Kobold for a troublesome spirit, and the name became attached to ores that frustrated their attempts to extract useful metal.1

In Saxony, miners tried smelting what they believed was silver-bearing ore. When it failed to yield the silver they expected, they blamed goblins for bewitching it. Some cobalt ores also contained arsenic, which could be released as poisonous fumes during processing. The material was dangerous as well as disappointing.12

In the eighteenth century, the Swedish chemist Georg Brandt investigated a similar ore and identified a previously unrecognized metal. The miners’ name was carried over to the element.2

Cobalt compounds give glass and ceramics a deep blue color. The name used for that familiar blue preserves the miners’ much less welcome experience of the ore.1

The potter used cobalt to color the glaze.

Sources

  1. Cobalt — Royal Society of Chemistry, Chemistry in its element
  2. Cobalt — Royal Society of Chemistry, Education

item.title: sandwich
item.description: Sandwich takes its name from John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich. The familiar gambling story is uncertain; the word appears in Edward Gibbon’s journal in 1762.
item.content:encoded:
On November 24, 1762, Edward Gibbon recorded an evening at a London club where men were eating sandwiches. His journal provides an early written record of the food’s English name, already familiar enough to use without explaining it.1

The name is traced to John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich. The familiar account has him eating beef between slices of bread so that he could carry on gambling without leaving the table. It comes from the French travel writer Pierre-Jean Grosley, who visited London in 1765 and later described a minister spending twenty-four hours at a game with little else to eat.2

That account is difficult to confirm. Grosley was passing on a story, and the evidence for Montagu as a compulsive gambler is weak. His biographer N. A. M. Rodger suggested that eating while working at his desk might explain the association instead. That remains a suggestion too.2

Gibbon’s entry shows the name in use before Grosley’s visit. The meal that first attached the earl’s title to the food is harder to recover.12

He packed a cheese sandwich for the journey.

Sources

  1. Discover the History of the Sandwich — PBS Food
  2. Sandwich — Dave Wilton, Wordorigins.org

item.title: text
item.description: Text and textile share the Latin verb texere, to weave. Latin textus carried the image of woven material into the structure of a written work.
item.content:encoded:
A text has a history of weaving. The Latin verb texere meant to weave or join things together. From it came textus, something woven, which was also used for the style or texture of a work.1

The image passed into writing. Late Latin used textus for a written account, and medieval usage included the Scriptures and other written works. English acquired text through French in the late fourteenth century, when it could mean the wording of something written or an authoritative passage.1

Textile comes from the same Latin verb, through textilis, meaning woven. The relationship between the two English words is easy to overlook because one belongs to writing and the other to fabric. Both retain the older idea of separate strands being joined into something continuous.2

She read the text again and added a note in the margin.

Sources

  1. Text — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Textile — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: culture
item.description: Culture began with cultivation and care. Cicero used cultura animi for the cultivation of the mind, extending an image rooted in tending the land.
item.content:encoded:
The Latin cultura meant cultivation or tending. It came from colere, a verb used for working the land and caring for things. The connection with agriculture was already a metaphor in Roman writing. Cicero used cultura animi, the cultivation of the mind.1

English borrowed culture in the fifteenth century for the working of land. By about 1500, it could also describe the development of the mind through education.2

In the nineteenth century it came to mean intellectual and artistic life, and the shared customs and achievements of a people. In a laboratory, microorganisms grown in a suitable environment are also called a culture.2

Food is an important part of the region’s culture.

Sources

  1. Culture — Raymond Williams, Keywords
  2. Culture — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: petrichor
item.description: Petrichor names the earthy smell associated with rain after dry weather. Two researchers formed the word from stone and the fluid of the Greek gods.
item.content:encoded:
Petrichor is the earthy smell associated with rain after a dry spell. The word joins Greek petra, stone, with ichor, the fluid said to flow in the veins of the gods.1

The name appeared in a 1964 paper by Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas, researchers at Australia’s CSIRO. Their article, Nature of Argillaceous Odour, was published in Nature on March 7.2

The smell was familiar long before it had a scientific name. Indian perfumers had already captured an earthy scent in sandalwood oil. By steam-distilling rocks that had been exposed to warm, dry conditions, Bear and Thomas obtained a yellowish oil associated with the odor, which moisture helped release.1

Petrichor drifted through the open window when the rain began.

Sources

  1. The smell of rain: how our scientists invented a new word — CSIRO
  2. Nature of Argillaceous Odour — I. J. Bear and R. G. Thomas, Nature, 1964

item.title: silhouette
item.description: Silhouette comes from the name of a French finance minister. The inexpensive profile portraits could be made quickly and sent to distant friends.
item.content:encoded:
A silhouette shows a figure by its outline, usually filled with a single dark color. The word comes from Étienne de Silhouette, who briefly served as France’s finance minister in 1759.1

One explanation connects the name with his unpopular economies. Cheap or spare things were mockingly described as à la Silhouette, and the name became attached to inexpensive profile portraits. Other explanations refer to his short time in office, so the precise reason for the association remains uncertain.12

A likeness of this kind could be cut from paper or painted quickly, cost relatively little, and travel easily in a letter.2

Photography later offered another affordable way to keep a likeness, and silhouette portraits became less fashionable.12

She recognized his silhouette at the window.

Sources

  1. Silhouette — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Q and Art: Silhouettes — Smithsonian American Art Museum

item.title: biscuit
item.description: Biscuit originally meant bread baked twice to dry it for keeping. The word now names quite different foods in Britain and America.
item.content:encoded:
The word biscuit once described how the food was made. Early French pain bescuit meant bread cooked twice. A second baking dried it out, helping it keep on a long journey. The phrase was shortened, and English borrowed the name.1

Ship’s biscuits became a staple of life at sea. They could be so hard that biting into them was difficult, and stored supplies were vulnerable to insects. Royal Museums Greenwich shows a surviving biscuit with holes made by biscuit beetles.2 Its collection also includes a biscuit made to an 1846 recipe.3

The word eventually covered foods made without a second baking. In Britain, a biscuit is usually what Americans call a cookie. In the United States, it commonly means a small, soft quick bread. The old cooking instruction remains in the name of both.1

She split a warm biscuit and spread it with butter.

Sources

  1. Biscuit — Merriam-Webster
  2. How to make a ship’s biscuit — Royal Museums Greenwich
  3. Ship’s biscuit — Royal Museums Greenwich, collection object AAB0766

item.title: tulip
item.description: Tulip traces back through Turkish tülbent to Persian dulband, a turban. Early botanical texts compare the flower with a head covering.
item.content:encoded:
The name of the tulip goes back through European languages to Turkish tülbent, borrowed from Persian dulband, meaning a turban. Tulip and turban are related words.1

The Turkish name of the flower is lale. How a word for a head covering became its name elsewhere has attracted several explanations. One is that the flower was thought to resemble a turban. Another concerns the practice of wearing tulips on turbans and a supposed confusion between the flower and the thing beneath it.2

The comparison with a head covering appears in sixteenth-century botanical writing. Johannes Kentmann’s notes link the flower’s shape with a Dalmatian cap. John Gerard later describes petals turning back as the flower opens, giving it the appearance of a Dalmatian or Turkish cap.3

A 2022 study examined these early texts. Its authors found the comparison, but no sixteenth-century evidence for the familiar story of a translator mixing up the names. The connection with a turban is well established; the conversation sometimes offered to explain it remains unconfirmed.13

The first tulip opened beside the garden wall.

Sources

  1. Tulip — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Tiptoe through the tulips: cultural history, molecular phylogenetics and classification of Tulipa — Christenhusz and colleagues, Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society, 2013
  3. Tracing the introduction history of the tulip that went wild in sixteenth-century Europe — Scientific Reports, 2022

item.title: dunce
item.description: Dunce comes from the name of John Duns Scotus, a respected medieval thinker whose followers later became targets of academic ridicule.
item.content:encoded:
To call someone a dunce is to call them slow to learn. The word comes from John Duns Scotus, a medieval philosopher admired for the subtlety of his thinking.1

Scotus studied and taught at major European universities. His lectures on Peter Lombard’s Sentences, a central work of medieval theology, became a widely read commentary. Glasgow University Library holds a printed edition from 1477, nearly 170 years after his death.2

His reputation changed as humanism gained ground in the sixteenth century. Followers who defended his teaching were ridiculed for resisting the new learning. Duns, a name associated with a school of thought, became a term of contempt. It acquired the spelling dunce and broadened into an insult for someone considered incapable of learning.12

He felt like a dunce when he finally understood the instructions.

Sources

  1. Dunce — Merriam-Webster
  2. 1477 edition of Duns Scotus’s Commentary on Lombard’s Sentences — University of Glasgow Library, Special Collections

item.title: pamphlet
item.description: Pamphlet takes its name from a medieval Latin poem. The small booklets later carried political arguments and installments of novels.
item.content:encoded:
The word comes from Pamphilus, seu de Amore, a popular Latin poem about love written in the twelfth century. Copies circulated as small booklets, and a form of the title gradually became a name for short works of this kind. Pamphilus was the central character’s name.12

The word was already in use for handwritten works before printing reached England. Printed pamphlets later carried political arguments and news, often cheaply enough to reach readers who could afford few books.2

The format also served fiction. Dickens’s David Copperfield appeared in monthly parts bound in paper wrappers. Those installments belong to the history of pamphlet binding too. A small folded publication could carry a public dispute or another portion of a novel whose readers were still waiting to learn what happened next.3

Someone had left a pamphlet on every seat.

Sources

  1. Pamphlet — Opening Artists’ Books, University of Utah Library
  2. Pamphlets in Early Modern England — The Map of Early Modern London, University of Victoria
  3. Pamphlet Bindings: A History & DIY Activity — University of Illinois Library Conservation Lab

item.title: apron
item.description: Apron began as napron. Speakers divided a napron as an apron, while Scots and northern English dialects preserved the older initial n.
item.content:encoded:
English once had napron, borrowed from French naperon, a word for a small cloth. In English it came to mean a covering worn over clothes to protect them.1

Say “a napron” aloud. The same sounds can be divided as “an apron.” Over time, speakers attached the initial n to the article, and the shortened form became established. Edinburgh records from 1508 already contain the spelling apronis.12

The older form survived elsewhere. The Dictionaries of the Scots Language records napron and related spellings with their initial n intact, and notes their use in northern English dialects too. The change spread unevenly, leaving different versions of the same word in use.3

She wiped the flour from her hands onto her apron.

Sources

  1. Apron — Merriam-Webster
  2. Aproun — Dictionaries of the Scots Language, Older Scottish Tongue
  3. Napron — Dictionaries of the Scots Language, Scottish National Dictionary

item.title: gossip
item.description: Gossip once meant a godparent or close companion. Shakespeare’s plays preserve both the older sense and the later insult.
item.content:encoded:
A gossip was once someone connected to a family through baptism. The Old English word godsibb joined God with kinship and referred to a godparent. Its meaning widened to include a close friend or companion.12

Several meanings were still in use in Shakespeare’s time. In Henry VIII, the king addresses his daughter’s godparents as “My noble gossips.” In Titus Andronicus, Aaron calls the nurse “a long-tongued, babbling gossip.” One use belongs to a christening ceremony. The other expresses distrust of someone who might reveal a secret.34

The word also became associated with women attending a birth and with the conversation at those gatherings. Its familiar sense developed alongside older meanings that remained available to speakers and writers.2

He was a terrible gossip, though everyone told him things.

Sources

  1. Gossip — Merriam-Webster
  2. Gossip and Gossips — The Map of Early Modern London, University of Victoria
  3. Henry VIII, Act 5, scene 4 — Folger Shakespeare Library
  4. Titus Andronicus, Act 4, scene 2 — Folger Shakespeare Library

item.title: museum
item.description: Museum comes from a Greek place of the Muses. In antiquity the name could belong to a place of learning and research, not only a collection of objects.
item.content:encoded:
A museum keeps and studies objects and makes them available to visitors. Its name goes back to the Greek Mouseion, a place connected with the Muses.12

In antiquity, such a place could be a shrine, a school or a place of study. The Museum at Alexandria housed scholars who worked there, with a common dining hall and places to walk and talk.2 The city’s famous library was closely tied to it, though sources differ on whether it was part of the Museum or a separate institution.23

The modern museum still studies what it holds. The definition the International Council of Museums adopted in 2022 names research, collecting and conservation alongside exhibition.4

The museum has a collection of old maps.

Sources

  1. Museum — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. Museum — Oxford Classical Dictionary
  3. Library of Alexandria — Encyclopædia Britannica
  4. Museum Definition — International Council of Museums

item.title: climate
item.description: Climate goes back to a Greek word for inclination. It once marked zones by the angle of the sun before it named their long-term weather.
item.content:encoded:
Climate now means the usual weather conditions of a place over a long time. The word began with an angle.12

The Greek klima meant an inclination. Ancient geographers divided the earth into zones by latitude and the angle of the sun’s rays. Places at similar latitudes received the noon sun at a similar angle, and were placed in the same zone.13

Weather came to define the word more fully. Rain, wind, altitude, and local geography also matter to a place’s climate.3

The island has a mild climate.

Sources

  1. Climate and Culture in Enlightenment Thought — James Rodger Fleming, Oxford Academic (1998)
  2. Climate — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  3. Climate – an introduction — UK Met Office (2023)

item.title: camera
item.description: Camera meant a room. In a camera obscura, light entering a dark chamber cast an image inside; the name later went to the device that recorded it.
item.content:encoded:
A camera records an image. The word comes from the Latin for a room or chamber.1

In a camera obscura, a darkened room or box, light enters through a small opening or lens. An image of the outside appears on the surface opposite. It can be viewed or traced onto paper.2

Some versions were large enough to enter; others were boxes an artist could take outside. Later, photographic materials made it possible to preserve the image instead of drawing it by hand.3

When photography developed, the shortened name went to the device that recorded the image.34

He left his camera on the table.

Sources

  1. Camera — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. Camera obscura — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  3. Introduction to the Camera Obscura — National Science and Media Museum
  4. Camera — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: lens
item.description: An optical lens was named for its resemblance to a lentil. The Latin lens meant the seed before it named the glass.
item.content:encoded:
A lens bends light so that an image can be seen or made. The word first named something that could be eaten.1

In Latin, lens meant a lentil. A lens that curves outward on both sides has much the same shape as the seed. That resemblance gave the piece of glass its name.1

She changed the lens on her camera.

Sources

  1. Lens — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language

item.title: muscle
item.description: Muscle comes from Latin musculus, little mouse. A flexing muscle may have suggested an animal moving under the skin.
item.content:encoded:
A muscle contracts to move part of the body. Its name comes from the Latin musculus, a little mouse.1

The likely image is a muscle moving under the skin when someone flexes, with its tendon suggesting a tail. The comparison is easy to test on an arm, though the reason for the name is given as probable rather than certain.2

The muscle in his arm tightened.

Sources

  1. Muscle — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. Words with Remarkable Origins — Merriam-Webster

item.title: emoji
item.description: Emoji is Japanese for picture character. Early Japanese phone networks had their own sets before Unicode helped make them readable across devices.
item.content:encoded:
An emoji is a picture character used in a message. Its name is Japanese: e means picture, and moji means character. The word has no etymological connection to the English emotion.1

Emoji were used on Japanese mobile phones before they became familiar around the world. Different phone companies had their own sets and their own ways of encoding them. A symbol sent from one network could fail to appear as intended on another.2

Unicode brought many of those characters into a common standard in 2010. A word from Japanese phones now names pictures that can travel between devices almost anywhere.2

She ended the message with a laughing emoji.

Sources

  1. FAQ: Emoji & Pictographs — Unicode Consortium
  2. Unicode Technical Standard #51: Unicode Emoji — Unicode Consortium

item.title: decimate
item.description: Decimate once meant selecting one soldier in ten for punishment. The Roman practice was far less routine than the word’s origin can make it sound.
item.content:encoded:
To decimate a group is to kill or destroy a large part of it. The word holds a more exact number from an older use: ten.1

The Latin decimare meant to punish every tenth person. Accounts of Roman military discipline describe soldiers chosen by lot, one in ten, from a disgraced unit and put to death.12

That does not mean Roman commanders routinely killed a tenth of their men. The evidence for its use in the Republic is sparse, and a study of the practice argues that it was revived in the late Republic after long periods without it.2

Today decimate usually means to devastate, even when the loss is much more than ten percent. The tenth remains in the word, though it is no longer a rule for using it.1

The disease decimated the herd.

Sources

  1. Decimate — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. Decimatio: Myth, Discipline, and Death in the Roman Republic — Michael J. Taylor, Antichthon, Cambridge University Press (2022)

item.title: quixotic
item.description: Quixotic comes from Don Quixote, the literary character whose pursuit of noble goals could take little account of the world around him.
item.content:encoded:
A quixotic plan is driven by an ideal that may be impossible to carry out. The adjective comes from a character in a book.1

Don Quixote, in Miguel de Cervantes’s novel, sets out to live as a knight. He sees a world of quests and enemies where other people see ordinary things. When he spots windmills on a plain, he takes them for giants. Sancho Panza tells him what they are, but Quixote charges them anyway. After he falls, he decides an enchanter must have turned the giants into windmills.2

His name first became a word for a person like him, a Quixote, and then an adjective. Quixotic can admire someone’s commitment to a noble aim while questioning whether the aim can be reached.1

The plan to restore every abandoned house was quixotic.

Sources

  1. Quixotic — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. Don Quixote, chapter VIII — Biblioteca Virtual Miguel de Cervantes

item.title: mentor
item.description: Mentor was a character in the Odyssey. Athena took his form to guide Telemachus; a later French novel helped turn his name into a common noun.
item.content:encoded:
A mentor is someone who guides a less experienced person. The word was a person’s name first.1

In Homer’s Odyssey, Mentor was a trusted friend of Odysseus. When Athena went to help Odysseus’s son Telemachus, she appeared in Mentor’s form. The advice came from the goddess, though the young man saw his father’s friend.12

Mentor took on a larger role in François Fénelon’s 1699 novel Les aventures de Télémaque. After that book, his name became a general word for a trusted guide in French and then in English.2

Her first editor became her mentor.

Sources

  1. Mentor — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. Word of the Day: mentor — Merriam-Webster

item.title: serendipity
item.description: Horace Walpole coined serendipity in a letter of 1754, after a story whose princes found things they had not gone looking for.
item.content:encoded:
Serendipity is the ability to find good things by accident. The word can also mean such a find itself.1

In a letter dated January 28, 1754, Horace Walpole wrote about a painting. In the same letter he described a discovery he had made about a Venetian coat of arms while looking through an old book at random. He said this discovery was almost of the kind he called serendipity.12

He took the word from the title of a fairy tale, The Three Princes of Serendip. Serendip was an old name for Sri Lanka. As the princes traveled, they kept finding things they had not set out to find, by chance and by their own good sense.12

Walpole’s word held both parts of the story: the accident, and the judgment to see what the accident had brought.12

Finding that letter in the archive was pure serendipity.

Sources

  1. Serendipity — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. The creation of the word ‘serendipity’ — Strawberry Hill House & Garden

item.title: bankruptcy
item.description: Bankruptcy is built on bankrupt, which came from the Italian banca rotta, a broken bench. Whether a bench was ever actually broken is another matter.
item.content:encoded:
Bankruptcy is what happens when someone cannot pay what they owe. It is built on bankrupt, which came into English from the Italian banca rotta: a broken bench.12

The bench is real. Banca was the ordinary Italian word for the table a money dealer worked at, and it is the same word that gave us bank. Rotta is broken, from the Latin rumpere.2

The breaking is the story. A dealer who could not meet his debts had his table broken in front of him, and that was the end of his trade. Samuel Johnson retold it in his dictionary of 1755.23

Nobody has produced evidence that it happened. The reading the dictionaries settle on is that rotta is figurative here, in the way an English business is said to be broken, and that no carpentry was involved. I could not confirm the custom.12

Breaking the instrument of an office was a real way of ending one. A degraded knight had his belt cut, his spurs struck off and his sword broken over his head; a Garter knight’s banner was pulled down and thrown out of the chapel; and judges have snapped the nib of the pen that signed a death sentence, on the reasoning that it should not be used again.45

Nothing I found joins any of that to the money dealer’s table. It does explain why the table is easy to picture: a reader who knows that a broken sword ends a knighthood will read a broken bench the same way.

The company filed for bankruptcy.

Sources

  1. Bankrupt — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Bankrupt — Michael Quinion, World Wide Words
  3. A Dictionary of the English Language, 1755 — Samuel Johnson, Internet Archive
  4. Degradation of a Garter Knight — College of St George, Windsor Castle
  5. The Unbroken Nib — LiveLaw

item.title: zero
item.description: Zero goes back to the Arabic sifr, empty. The same word entered Europe twice and came out as two English words: zero and cipher.
item.content:encoded:
Zero is nothing, written down. The word goes back to the Arabic sifr, empty, which was itself used to render the Sanskrit śūnya, empty—the name Indian mathematicians gave the mark that held an empty place.12

Europe took the word twice. One route latinised it as cifra, which gave English cipher; the other, through Fibonacci’s zephirum, gave Italian zefiro and then zero.123

So the two are the same word arriving by different roads. Cipher carried both senses into English: zero, in its older use, and a code.3

The total came to zero.

Sources

  1. Zero — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. A History of Zero — MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews
  3. Cipher — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: yacht
item.description: Yacht is the Dutch jacht, from jagen, to hunt or chase: a fast boat built to catch pirates, before it had anything to do with leisure.
item.content:encoded:
A yacht is a boat for pleasure. The word is the Dutch jacht, shortened from jachtschip, hunting ship, from jagen, to hunt or chase.12

It was built for the chase. Dutch warships were too heavy to catch the pirates and smugglers working their coast, so lighter and faster craft were made to run them down.12

One was presented to Charles II in 1660, and he used it to go out on the water for the pleasure of it. English gentlemen wanted the same, and the word stopped meaning the chase.12

They spent August on a yacht.

Sources

  1. Yacht — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Yacht — Merriam-Webster

item.title: X-ray
item.description: Röntgen called the new rays X because nobody knew what they were. The X is the mathematician’s unknown, and it was never replaced.
item.content:encoded:
An X-ray is radiation used to see inside things. Wilhelm Röntgen found it in November 1895, working with a covered cathode-ray tube, and announced it in a short paper called On a New Kind of Rays.12

He called them X-rays. The X is the one from algebra, the letter you put where a quantity is not known yet. He did not know what the rays were and said so in the name.12

German and several other languages call them Röntgen rays instead. He preferred his own placeholder, and English kept it.12

The rays were explained long ago. The word still says nobody knows.1

The X-ray showed a hairline fracture.

Sources

  1. Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen: Biographical — The Nobel Prize
  2. Wilhelm Röntgen — Linda Hall Library

item.title: window
item.description: Window is the Old Norse vindauga, wind eye. It replaced Old English words that called the same hole an eye-hole and an eye-door.
item.content:encoded:
A window is a hole in a wall with glass in it. The word is the Old Norse vindauga, from vindr, wind, and auga, eye: the wind’s eye.12

It came into English in the early thirteenth century and named what there was then—an unglazed opening, often in a roof, that let in the weather along with the light. The wind is in the name because the wind came in.1

Old English had its own words for it: eagþyrl, eye-hole, and eagduru, eye-door. Both were replaced, but everyone involved had seen the same thing in it—an eye in a wall.1

She opened the window.

Sources

  1. Window — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Window — Merriam-Webster

item.title: utopia
item.description: Thomas More built Utopia in 1516 out of the Greek for no place. The island where everything is right is named for not existing.
item.content:encoded:
A utopia is an imagined society in which everything has been got right. Thomas More made the word up in 1516, as the name of the island in his book.12

He built it from the Greek ou, not, and topos, place: no place. The joke is that it is a syllable away from eu-topos, good place, and More points at it himself—an addendum to the book has a verse saying the island ought rightly to be called Eutopia, the place of happiness.12

Both readings sit in the word at once, and the book does not choose between them.1

Their plan was a utopia and everybody knew it.

Sources

  1. Utopia by Thomas More — Encyclopædia Britannica
  2. Utopia — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: trivia
item.description: Trivia is the Latin plural of trivium, the place where three roads meet. What was said at a crossroads was public, and then commonplace.
item.content:encoded:
Trivia are small facts of no great weight. The word is the Latin plural of trivium, the place where three roads meet.1

A crossroads is a public place. Anyone might be standing in it, and what was said there was what anyone might say, so trivialis came to mean public, and then ordinary, and then of no particular importance.1

The medieval university used the same word for the first three of the seven liberal arts—grammar, rhetoric and logic—the ones taken before the other four. To be trivial was to belong to that first stage.12

The sense the word has now, facts asked and answered for their own sake, is from the 1960s and American campuses.1

He is unbeatable at trivia.

Sources

  1. Trivia — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Trivium — Encyclopædia Britannica

item.title: rival
item.description: Rival comes from the Latin rivalis, from rivus, a stream: the people who drew water from the same watercourse.
item.content:encoded:
A rival is someone competing with you for the same thing. The word comes from the Latin rivalis, from rivus, a stream.12

Rivales were the people who took water from the same watercourse. It was a legal relationship before it was a hostile one: Roman law had provisions for what to do when two of them disagreed.12

The water fell away as the word moved through French into English in the later sixteenth century. The competition stayed, mostly over love or honour rather than irrigation.12

The shape of the old sense is still there. A rival is an opponent who draws on the same supply you do.12

He was her closest rival.

Sources

  1. Rival — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. The History of ‘Rival’ — Merriam-Webster

item.title: nostalgia
item.description: Nostalgia was coined in a medical dissertation of 1688, from the Greek nostos, homecoming, and algos, pain. It was the name of an illness.
item.content:encoded:
Nostalgia is a fond feeling about the past. It started as the name of an illness.12

Johannes Hofer, a medical student at Basel, made the word for his dissertation of 1688 out of the Greek nostos, homecoming, and algos, pain. It was his Latin for the German Heimweh, homesickness, and he described it as a disease of the brain.12

The patients were often Swiss mercenaries serving abroad, set off by a remembered sight or a tune from home. They stopped eating and sleeping. It was taken seriously enough to be treated, and seriously enough to be written down as a cause of death.3

The word softened as the illness stopped being one. The ache stayed. The algos is half the word.12

A wave of nostalgia for the nineties.

Sources

  1. Johannes Hofer — Encyclopædia Britannica
  2. Nostalgia — Online Etymology Dictionary
  3. The Soldiers Who Died of Homesickness — The Conversation

item.title: melancholy
item.description: Melancholy is the Greek melankholia, black bile. It names the fluid that was held to cause the mood, in a medicine nobody practises now.
item.content:encoded:
Melancholy is a settled, quiet sadness. The word is the Greek melankholia, from melas, black, and kholē, bile.12

It began as a diagnosis. In the medicine that ran from Hippocrates through Galen and on into the eighteenth century, the body held four humours—blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile—and the mixture of them made a person’s temperament. Too much black bile made you melancholy.12

There is no black bile. The humours were abandoned and the treatments went with them, but the word outlived the physiology it was built on.12

A melancholy that lasted all winter.

Sources

  1. Melancholy — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. What is Melancholy? — Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh

item.title: lecture
item.description: Lecture comes from the Medieval Latin lectura, a reading. In the medieval university it was exactly that: the book read out to students who had no copy.
item.content:encoded:
A lecture is a talk given in order to teach something. The word comes from the Medieval Latin lectura, a reading, from legere, to read.12

It meant that literally. In the medieval university the teacher read out of the book and the students wrote it down, because there was one book, it was expensive, and they did not have it.1

The sense of a discourse on a subject, rather than a reading out of a text, appears in the 1530s. Printing had been at work for two generations by then.1

A lecture is now an exposition, and often anything but a reading. The word still names the older arrangement: a room with one copy of the book in it.12

The lecture was at nine on Monday.

Sources

  1. Lecture — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Lecture — Middle English Compendium, University of Michigan

item.title: juggernaut
item.description: Juggernaut is an English rendering of Jagannath, whose temple cars at Puri are vast and hard to stop. The horror the word carries was supplied by missionary accounts.
item.content:encoded:
A juggernaut is a force that flattens whatever is in front of it. The word is an English rendering of Jagannath, a deity of eastern India whose name means lord of the universe.1

One part of the image is plain enough. At the Rath Yatra in Puri, enormous chariots carrying the deities are pulled through the streets by hundreds of people, and something that heavy is genuinely hard to stop or steer once it is moving.1

The rest was supplied. Claudius Buchanan, an Anglican chaplain who had seen the festival, published Christian Researches in Asia in 1811; it became one of the most widely read English accounts of India of its day. He wrote the procession up as a scene of heathen horror, in support of the case for Christian missions, and that is the book the English word came through.2

English kept the crushing and left the rest behind.12

The company became a juggernaut.

Sources

  1. The Origins of the Juggernaut — Anatoly Liberman, OUPblog, Oxford University Press
  2. Buchanan, Claudius (1766–1815) — History of Missiology, Boston University School of Theology

item.title: inaugurate
item.description: Inaugurate comes from the Latin inaugurare, to consecrate by augury: to install someone once the omens had been read in the birds.
item.content:encoded:
To inaugurate is to install someone in office, or to open something formally. The word comes from the Latin inaugurare, built on augur.12

An augur was a Roman priest who read the will of the gods in birds: how they flew, how they fed, what they called. The job was to find out whether the gods approved of a thing being started at all. It was not a way of predicting what would happen.12

So a man was inaugurated—installed once the birds had been consulted and the answer was yes. Nothing of consequence was begun without it.2

Presidents are still inaugurated. The birds dropped out of the ceremony and stayed in the word.1

The new building was inaugurated in May.

Sources

  1. Inaugurate — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. The Origin of ‘Inaugurate’ — Merriam-Webster

item.title: idiot
item.description: Idiot comes from the Greek idiōtēs, a private person: someone who held no office and took no part in public affairs.
item.content:encoded:
An idiot is a fool. The word comes from the Greek idiōtēs, from idios, one’s own, private. An idiōtēs was a private person: not in the public eye, holding no office.12

It said nothing about intelligence. It described what a person did not take part in. From there the word went to the common man, and from the common man to the ignorant one, since ordinary people were not generally the ones with the learning.12

English took it in that ignorant sense and then narrowed it again, from a man without education to a man without sense.2

Some idiot had left the gate open.

Sources

  1. Idiot — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Idiot — Merriam-Webster

item.title: farce
item.description: Farce comes from the Latin farcire, to stuff. It meant forcemeat first, then the comic matter stuffed in among the scenes of a religious play.
item.content:encoded:
A farce is a comedy of slammed doors and mistaken identity. Said of anything else, it is a thing that has stopped being serious. It comes from the Latin farcire, to stuff or cram. English borrowed it first in the fourteenth century, and it meant forcemeat: the stuffing itself.12

The theatre took the word from the kitchen. Phrases were stuffed into the fixed words of the liturgy at festivals, and the same word was then used for the comic business stuffed in among the scenes of a religious play.12

The stuffing grew into a form of its own. English borrowed the word a second time in the sixteenth century, and that time it meant the comedy.2

The trial was a farce.

Sources

  1. Farce — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. The Culinary Roots of ‘Farce’ — Merriam-Webster

item.title: eavesdrop
item.description: The eavesdrop was the strip of ground where rain fell off a roof. Someone standing in it, against the wall, was an eavesdropper.
item.content:encoded:
To eavesdrop is to listen to something you are not part of. The word was a place before it was an act.1

The eavesdrop, or eavesdrip, was the strip of ground around a building where the rain came off the eaves. Old English had it as yfesdrype, and it mattered in law: you could not build too near your neighbour’s boundary, because your roof would drain onto their land.12

Anyone standing in that strip is standing against the wall, under the eaves, close enough to hear what is said inside. By the fifteenth century that person had a name. The verb came later, out of the name.12

He was eavesdropping on the next table.

Sources

  1. Eavesdrop — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Eavesdrop — Wordorigins.org

item.title: bank
item.description: Bank comes from the Italian banca, a bench: the counter a money-changer worked at. Bankrupt is built from the same table.
item.content:encoded:
A bank is an institution that holds money. The word comes from the Italian banca, a bench, which was also used for the bench-like counter a money-changer worked at, and then for the shop itself.12

The trade travelled from Italy to France and England and the word went with it. The marble hall and the application on a phone both started as a table in a market.2

The bank refused the loan.

Sources

  1. Bank — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Bank — Merriam-Webster

item.title: sabotage
item.description: Sabotage comes from sabot, a wooden shoe, but not from throwing one into a machine. The clog story is recorded nowhere.
item.content:encoded:
Sabotage is damage done on purpose to stop something working. It is a French word, taken into English early in the twentieth century, from sabot, a wooden shoe or clog.12

The story everybody knows is that workers threw their clogs into the machinery. It is repeated everywhere and recorded nowhere: no account of anyone actually doing it has been produced.2

The likelier route is duller and stays inside the language. French saboter meant to clatter about in wooden shoes, and from there to work clumsily, and from there to botch a job on purpose.12

The clog is in the word either way. Nobody can show that one was ever thrown into a machine.2

The line was shut down by sabotage.

Sources

  1. Sabotage — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Sabotage — Wordorigins.org

item.title: assassin
item.description: Assassin comes from hashishi, a term of abuse used against the Nizari Ismailis. The hashish story that travelled to Europe with it is a legend.
item.content:encoded:
An assassin kills someone prominent, usually for political reasons. The word came into European languages from variants of the Arabic hashishi, plural hashishiyya.1

It was not a description. Other Muslims used it against the Nizari Ismailis as an insult, in the sense of low-class rabble or people of lax morals, with no claim attached that they used the drug.1

The literal reading came later, and from outside. Crusader-era reports and then Marco Polo told of an Old Man of the Mountain who drugged young men and showed them a garden of paradise so they would kill on command. Farhad Daftary’s work on those accounts traces them to European invention and rumour rather than to anything recorded at Alamut.12

The legend crossed into English and took the word with it. The drug is still in the name, and nobody has been able to show it was ever there.12

He was killed by an assassin.

Sources

  1. Assassin — The Institute of Ismaili Studies
  2. Introduction to The Assassin Legends — Farhad Daftary, The Institute of Ismaili Studies

item.title: salary
item.description: Salary comes from the Latin salarium, formed from sal, salt. The familiar claim that Roman soldiers were paid in salt is in no ancient source.
item.content:encoded:
A salary is what you are paid for your work. It came through French from the Latin salarium, which is formed from sal, salt. That much is not in dispute.1

The story attached to it is that Roman soldiers were paid in salt, and the story has a source. Pliny the Elder, writing in the first century, says salt is bound up with public honours and military service, and that salarium is named from it.2

That is all he says. He does not write that soldiers were paid in salt, and no other ancient writer does either. The sentence about legions receiving salt instead of coin appears to be a later addition, filled in by dictionary-makers who wanted the connection to mean something definite.3

So the salt is genuinely in the word and the reason for it is missing. I could not find an ancient source for the payment, and the scholarship says there is none to find.23

She took a cut in salary.

Sources

  1. Salary — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Natural History, Book XXXI, chapter 41 — Pliny the Elder, Perseus Digital Library, Tufts University
  3. Salt and Salary: Were Roman Soldiers Paid in Salt? — Peter Gainsford, Kiwi Hellenist

item.title: pupil
item.description: The pupil of the eye is the Latin pupilla, little doll: the small figure of yourself you can see reflected in it.
item.content:encoded:
The pupil of the eye is the dark opening in the middle of the iris. The word is the Latin pupilla, a little doll, a diminutive of pupa, girl or doll.12

It is named after what you see in it. Stand close enough to someone and there is a tiny figure of you in their eye, about doll-sized. Greek did the same thing with korē, girl, which meant both the doll and the pupil.1

The schoolchild comes from the same Latin root by another road. Pupillus and pupilla also meant an orphan or a minor in someone’s care, and the English pupil began as that legal sense before it meant anyone being taught.12

The doctor checked his pupils.

Sources

  1. Pupil — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Pupil — Merriam-Webster

item.title: lunatic
item.description: Lunatic comes from the Latin luna, moon, and the belief that madness followed the moon’s phases. It stayed in English law until 1930.
item.content:encoded:
A lunatic is a madman, in the loose and old-fashioned way the word is used now. It comes from the Latin luna, moon, through the Late Latin lunaticus, moon-struck.1

The idea behind it was a medical one: that some kinds of madness came and went with the phases of the moon, and that the moon was what moved them.1

The belief went, and the word stayed in the law long after it. English statutes used lunatic as a legal category into the twentieth century, and it was the Mental Treatment Act of 1930 that turned lunatics, officially, into patients.2

Nobody who uses the word now is thinking about the moon.

Some lunatic overtook us on the bend.

Sources

  1. Lunacy — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. 90 Years Ago: the Mental Treatment Act 1930 — Claire Hilton, Royal College of Psychiatrists

item.title: algebra
item.description: Algebra comes from al-jabr in the title of al-Khwarizmi’s ninth-century book: the restoring of something broken, a bone included.
item.content:encoded:
Algebra comes from the Arabic al-jabr, out of the title of a book al-Khwarizmi wrote in Baghdad in the ninth century, Hisab al-jabr w’al-muqabala.1

Al-jabr is restoring, or reuniting what is broken. In the book it names a particular move: a term subtracted on one side is restored by adding it to the other, until the equation balances.12

The everyday sense travelled with the word. When algebra first came into English in the sixteenth century it could still mean the surgical setting of a fracture, and in Spanish an algebrista was a bone-setter.3

The same book gave the other word. Algorithm came out of the author’s name.1

He teaches algebra to first-year students.

Sources

  1. Al-Khwarizmi — MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews
  2. The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing — Encyclopædia Britannica
  3. Algebra — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: turquoise
item.description: Turquoise is the Old French for Turkish: pierre turqueise, the Turkish stone. It is named for the route it arrived by, not the ground it came out of.
item.content:encoded:
Turquoise is a blue-green stone, and since the nineteenth century a colour as well. The name comes from the Old French turqueise, Turkish, in the phrase pierre turqueise: the Turkish stone.1

The stone was not Turkish. The finest of it was mined in Persia, and Europe knew it because Venetian merchants bought it in Turkish markets and the overland routes ran through Ottoman territory.12

So the name records the way it came rather than where it came from. The colour was named after the stone in the 1850s, and the colour is now what most people mean by the word: a country’s name, on a paint chart.1

The ring was set with turquoise.

Sources

  1. Turquoise — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Turquoise History and Lore — Gemological Institute of America

item.title: horde
item.description: Horde goes back to the Turkic ordu, a ruler’s camp and then any army. In English it came out meaning a disorderly crowd.
item.content:encoded:
A horde is a large, disorderly crowd. The word goes back to the Turkic ordu, camp or army: the ruler’s encampment first, and then any military one.12

It reached English in the 1550s by a long route, through Turkic into Russian and Polish and on westward. The h at the front appears to have been picked up in Polish.1

It travelled with the Golden Horde and the armies of the steppe, seen from outside and at a distance. By the 1610s the word was being used for any uncivilised gang.1

An ordu is an organised thing, with a chain of command and a place for everything. A horde is a rabble. The word travelled west and ended up meaning the opposite of what it started as.12

A horde of tourists filled the square.

Sources

  1. Horde — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Horde — Collins English Dictionary

item.title: magazine
item.description: Magazine comes from the Arabic makhzan, a storehouse. The ammunition store, the periodical and the part of a rifle are the same idea three times.
item.content:encoded:
A magazine is something you read. The word comes from the Arabic makhzan, a storehouse or depot, and reached English through French in the 1580s.1

Its first English sense was the literal one: a warehouse, and particularly a store of military supplies and ammunition.1

In 1731 Edward Cave started a monthly in London called The Gentleman’s Magazine, made up of pieces gathered from other publications. He meant the word as it sounds, a storehouse of writing, and it is the first periodical the word was used for.12

The rifle kept the older sense. The part that holds the cartridges is a magazine because it is where they are stored. The shelf at the newsagent and the box of ammunition are named for the same thing.1

The article ran in a monthly magazine.

Sources

  1. Magazine — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. The Gentleman’s Magazine — Encyclopædia Britannica

item.title: school
item.description: School came through the Latin schola from the Greek skholē, which meant spare time, leisure, rest.
item.content:encoded:
A school is a place people are taught in. The word came through the Latin schola from the Greek skholē, which meant spare time, leisure, rest.12

The connection is less odd than it looks. Free time was what you needed in order to sit and argue about something, so the word moved from the time to the discussion held in it, and then to the people holding the discussion and the place they held it in.12

Latin kept some of that width. Schola could mean leisure for learning, a lecture, a debate, or a place of learning.12

English took the narrowest of those senses: a building, a register and a timetable.1

She teaches at a school in the city.

Sources

  1. School — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Get Schooled on the Origins of ‘School’ — Merriam-Webster

item.title: malaria
