item.description: Malaria is the Italian mala aria, bad air. The disease was thought to rise off marshes as a vapour; the explanation went and the name stayed.
item.content:encoded:
Malaria is a disease carried by mosquitoes. The name is the Italian mala aria, bad air.1

It was named for what people believed caused it. Fevers were common around marshes, and the vapour coming off stagnant water was held to be what made people ill.12

The parasite was identified in 1880 and the mosquito was shown to carry it before the century was out. The air had nothing to do with it.2

The name did not change with the theory. We understand the disease now, and it is still called after an idea about air that nobody believes.1

Malaria is still one of the world’s deadliest diseases.

Sources

  1. Malaria — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Bad Air — Science History Institute

item.title: vaccine
item.description: Vaccine comes from the Latin vacca, cow. The first protection against smallpox was taken from cowpox, and the cow stayed in the name.
item.content:encoded:
A vaccine is a preparation that trains the body against a disease. The word comes from the Latin vacca, cow.12

Edward Jenner’s report of 1798 was an inquiry into the Variolae vaccinae, the pustules of the cow: his term for cowpox. People who had caught cowpox, usually from milking, turned out to be protected against smallpox.1

The method spread and the name went with it. Vaccines are made in many ways now and almost none of them involve a cow, but the word still says where the first one was found.12

The vaccine was given in two doses.

Sources

  1. Etymologia: Variola and Vaccination — Emerging Infectious Diseases, CDC
  2. Vaccine — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: ostracism
item.description: Ostracism comes from ostrakon, a potsherd. Athenians voted to banish a man by scratching his name on a piece of broken pottery.
item.content:encoded:
Ostracism is being shut out by the group you belong to. The word comes from the Greek ostrakon, a potsherd: a piece of broken pottery.1

An Athenian who wanted a man banished for ten years scratched his name on a sherd and handed it in. Broken pottery was everywhere, which is why the vote was taken on it.12

Thousands of those sherds have come out of the Agora and the Kerameikos, names still legible on them, most of them from refuse dumps.2

The procedure ended and the word kept only the exclusion. The object dropped out of it: a piece of rubbish with a name scratched on it.1

He faced ostracism from the whole village.

Sources

  1. Ostracism — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Ostraka from the Athenian Agora, 1970–1972 — Hesperia, American School of Classical Studies at Athens

item.title: curfew
item.description: Curfew comes from the Old French cuevrefeu, cover fire: an evening bell telling a town built of timber to bank its hearths for the night.
item.content:encoded:
A curfew is an order to be off the streets after a certain hour. The word comes from the Old French cuevrefeu, cover fire.1

In medieval towns built largely of timber, a bell rang in the evening and households banked or covered their hearths for the night. A fire left untended was everybody’s problem.12

The cover itself was called a curfew too: a lid of terracotta or metal put over the embers to hold them safely until morning.2

The bell stopped and the fire went out of the meaning. By the nineteenth century the word had become what it is now, an hour after which you have to be indoors.1

The city was under curfew.

Sources

  1. Curfew — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. The History of the Curfew — John Moore Museum, Tewkesbury

item.title: noon
item.description: Noon comes from the Latin nona hora, the ninth hour, which fell around three in the afternoon. The hour moved and the nine stayed.
item.content:encoded:
Noon is the middle of the day. The word comes from the Latin nona hora, the ninth hour, one of the fixed hours of prayer.12

Counted from around six in the morning, the ninth hour fell at about three in the afternoon. That is where noon was in English for a long time.12

Between the twelfth century and the fourteenth it moved to midday. Why is not settled. Unreliable clocks, daylight that stretches and shrinks with the northern seasons, and the fact that a day’s fast ended at nones have all been offered as reasons.12

Noon settled at twelve and stayed there. The hour it is named after is three hours later.

We’ll meet at noon.

Sources

  1. Noon — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. ‘Noon’: Not Always at Twelve O’Clock — Merriam-Webster

item.title: kiosk
item.description: Kiosk came into English through French from the Turkish köşk, an open garden pavilion. The word has been getting smaller ever since.
item.content:encoded:
A kiosk is a small stall you buy something at, or a screen you touch to print a ticket. It came into English through the French kiosque, from the Turkish köşk, and behind that the Persian kūshk.1

A köşk was a pavilion, open on some or all sides, built in a garden to be sat in. The Çinili Köşk at Topkapı, put up in 1472 under Mehmed II, was a pleasure pavilion in the outer gardens, used to watch the games and spectacles held in the square it faced.2

Europe borrowed the building first, in the seventeenth century, as ornament for parks and gardens. Then the word was handed down to smaller and smaller things: a newspaper stand by the 1860s, a telephone box in the 1920s, and now a machine bolted to the floor of an airport.1

She bought a ticket at the kiosk.

Sources

  1. Kiosk — Online Etymology Dictionary
  2. Çinili Köşk, İstanbul — Archnet, Aga Khan Documentation Center, MIT Libraries

item.title: consider
item.description: Consider comes from Latin considerare, to observe attentively or contemplate. It is probably connected with sidus, star or constellation, though the exact origin is not certain.
item.content:encoded:
To consider something is to think about it carefully.

The word comes through Old French from Latin considerare, to observe attentively or contemplate.12

A long-standing explanation connects the Latin verb with sidus, meaning a star, heavenly body, or constellation. On that reading, considerare may once have meant something like observing the stars closely, perhaps for navigation or divination.12

The connection is probable rather than certain. Other explanations for the Latin verb have been proposed, so the star story is best kept as a strong possibility rather than a literal definition.2

English kept the idea of close attention even after the stars disappeared from ordinary use.

I need some time to consider the offer.

Sources

  1. Consider — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. Consider — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: desire
item.description: Desire comes from Latin desiderare, to long for or feel the absence of something. A connection with sidus, star, is possible, but the exact history is uncertain.
item.content:encoded:
A desire is a feeling of wanting something.

English got the word through Old French from Latin desiderare. In Latin, the verb could mean to long for something, but also to miss it or feel its absence.12

There is a well-known explanation that connects desiderare with sidus, star or constellation. On that reading, the word may once have carried an idea connected with looking to the stars or waiting for what they would bring.12

The exact origin is not certain. Etymologists have proposed other explanations too, so the neat claim that desire simply means something like “from the stars” goes further than the evidence allows.2

What is secure is the older sense of longing for what is absent.

He had a strong desire to go home.

Sources

  1. Desire — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. Desire — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: companion
item.description: Companion comes through French from a Late Latin word formed from com-, together, and panis, bread: someone associated with sharing bread.
item.content:encoded:
A companion is someone who goes with you or spends time with you.

The word came through Old French from a Late Latin form built from com-, together, and panis, bread. Its older sense was a fellow or associate understood through the idea of sharing bread or a meal.12

The meaning widened into the familiar sense of a person who accompanies another. The bread is no longer part of the definition, but it is part of the word’s construction.12

She was his companion on the long journey.

Sources

  1. Companion — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. Companion — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: disaster
item.description: Disaster came through French from Italian disastro, built from a negative prefix and astro, star. One of its earliest senses concerned an unfavourable star or planet.
item.content:encoded:
A disaster is a catastrophe or serious misfortune.

The word came into English through French from Italian disastro. The second part comes from astro, star. One of the earliest English senses referred to an unfavourable influence or position of a star or planet.12

The word then settled into the broader meaning of a great misfortune or catastrophe. The astrological belief disappeared from ordinary use, but it remains in the word’s history.12

The storm became a disaster for the coastal towns.

Sources

  1. Disaster — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. The Secret Histories of ‘Catastrophe,’ ‘Debacle,’ and More — Merriam-Webster

item.title: candidate
item.description: Candidate comes from Latin candidatus, meaning white-robed. Roman men seeking public office were associated with a bright white toga.
item.content:encoded:
A candidate is someone being considered for a position, office, award, or other selection.

The word comes from Latin candidatus, meaning white-robed. In ancient Rome, a man seeking public office was associated with a bright white toga, and the word for the clothing became the word for the office-seeker.12

English later widened candidate beyond elections to people being considered for many kinds of positions or outcomes.1

She was one of three candidates for the position.

Sources

  1. Candidate — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. candidatus — Logeion, University of Chicago

item.title: robot
item.description: Robot entered international use through Karel Čapek’s play R.U.R. The word was suggested by his brother Josef from Czech robota, meaning forced labour or hard work.
item.content:encoded:
A robot is a machine that can carry out tasks automatically.

The word entered international use through Karel Čapek’s 1920 play R.U.R., where it named artificial workers. Čapek later credited his brother Josef with suggesting the word.12

Josef drew it from Czech robota, a word connected with forced labour, serf labour, or hard work. The labour was already in the name before the modern machine existed.12

The factory uses robots for welding.

Sources

  1. Čapek’s R.U.R. published in Filipino — Embassy of the Czech Republic in Manila
  2. Karel Čapek — Radio Prague International

item.title: algorithm
item.description: Algorithm ultimately comes from the name of the ninth-century mathematician al-Khwarizmi, whose work on calculation reached Europe in Latin translation.
item.content:encoded:
An algorithm is a set of steps for solving a problem or carrying out a calculation.

The word ultimately comes from the name of the ninth-century mathematician al-Khwarizmi. A Latin version of a work associated with him on Hindu-Arabic numerals used a form of his name, Algoritmi. That name gave rise to algorism, a word for arithmetic using those numerals.12

Over time, the spelling and meaning changed. Algorithm came to mean a defined procedure for calculation and then, more broadly, a step-by-step procedure for solving a problem.12

The search engine uses an algorithm to rank results.

Sources

  1. Al-Khwarizmi — MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews
  2. Arabic numerals — MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews

item.title: deadline
item.description: During the American Civil War, a dead line was a prison boundary prisoners were forbidden to cross. The modern time-limit sense may have been influenced by it.
item.content:encoded:
A deadline is the latest time by which something must be done.

During the American Civil War, dead line was used for a boundary inside some military prisons. Prisoners were forbidden to cross it, and guards could fire on those who did. Andersonville is the best-known example, but the National Park Service notes that such lines were used at several prisons.1

The modern sense of a final time limit appeared in American newspaper jargon by 1919. The older prison use may have influenced it, but the connection is not certain.2

The deadline is Friday.

Sources

  1. The Deadline — Andersonville National Historic Site, U.S. National Park Service
  2. Deadline — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: guy
item.description: Guy comes from Guy Fawkes. His name passed to effigies, then to strangely dressed men, and eventually to an everyday word for a person.
item.content:encoded:
A guy is an ordinary word for a man or, in some uses, a person.

The word comes from Guy Fawkes. Effigies of him burned on November 5 came to be called guys. The word then spread to people who looked strange or badly dressed.12

In American English, guy became a general word for a man, and the plural guys later widened further in everyday speech.12

He seems like a nice guy.

Sources

  1. Guy — Merriam-Webster
  2. The Life of Guy: Guy Fawkes, the Gunpowder Plot, and the Unlikely History of an Indispensable Word — Oxford Academic

item.title: maverick
item.description: Maverick first referred to unbranded cattle associated with Samuel Maverick. It later became a word for an independent person.
item.content:encoded:
A maverick is an independent person who does not follow the group.

The word comes from Samuel A. Maverick, a nineteenth-century Texas landowner. Unbranded cattle associated with him came to be called mavericks, and the word spread through cattle country for unbranded animals.12

By the end of the nineteenth century, the word was also being used for people who went their own way.12

She was a maverick in her field.

Sources

  1. Mavericks and Mavericking — Texas State Historical Association
  2. Maverick — Merriam-Webster, Word of the Day

item.title: boycott
item.description: Boycott comes from Charles Boycott, an English land agent in Ireland whose name became the term for organized refusal and social exclusion.
item.content:encoded:
To boycott something is to refuse to buy, use, or take part in it as a form of protest.

The word comes from Charles Boycott, an English land agent in County Mayo, Ireland. In 1880, during a dispute over rents and evictions, local people and members of the Irish Land League isolated him. Workers left, businesses refused to deal with him, and his name became attached to the tactic.12

The name spread quickly from one dispute to a general word for organized refusal.12

They agreed to boycott the company.

Sources

  1. Boycott — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language, Fifth Edition
  2. Boycott — Merriam-Webster, Word of the Day

item.title: broadcast
item.description: Before broadcast meant radio or television, it described seed scattered by hand over a wide area.
item.content:encoded:
To broadcast something is to send it out to many people.

The word was used first for scattering seed over a wide area, usually by hand. That agricultural sense is much older than radio.12

In the early twentieth century, broadcast was taken up for radio transmission. The older idea of sending something out widely was kept, but the seed had become a signal.2

The agricultural meaning still exists today.1

The interview was broadcast live.

Sources

  1. Broadcast — Merriam-Webster
  2. Broadcast — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: Rosetta stone
item.description: The Rosetta Stone gave scholars the key to Egyptian hieroglyphs. The name now means any clue that makes a difficult mystery possible to understand.
item.content:encoded:
A Rosetta stone is a clue or discovery that makes a difficult mystery possible to understand.

The original Rosetta Stone was found in Egypt in 1799. The same decree had been written on it in three scripts: Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Ancient Greek. Scholars could read the Greek. For the first time, they had a way to compare a known text with writing they could not yet read.1

Thomas Young made important early advances. In 1822, the French scholar Jean-François Champollion made the decisive breakthrough and showed that hieroglyphs could record the sounds of the Egyptian language.1

A replica stands in the NSA’s National Cryptologic Museum, in an exhibit on the work of the agency’s language analysts.2

The new evidence proved to be a Rosetta stone.

item.title: nightmare
item.description: The mare in nightmare is an old word for a spirit or demon believed to trouble sleepers. The horse is a different word.
item.content:encoded:
A nightmare is a bad dream. The mare in it is an old word for a spirit or demon once believed to trouble sleeping people. The horse is a different word.12

In the old belief, the mare oppressed the sleeper and brought a feeling of suffocation. The word later moved from the creature to the experience, and then to a frightening dream.2

The creature disappeared from belief, but the word stayed. Related forms survive in other Germanic languages too.2

It was a nightmare.

Sources

  1. Nightmare — The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language
  2. Nightmare — Online Etymology Dictionary

item.title: quarantine
item.description: Quarantine comes from the Italian quaranta, forty. In 1920 Russian refugees were kept in quarantine off İstanbul.
item.content:encoded:
Quarantine is a period of separation that keeps a disease from spreading. It comes from the Italian quaranta, forty.1

During the plague, ships arriving from infected places could be kept at anchor for forty days before anyone came ashore. The Italian for forty is quaranta. The period became quarantena.1

In 1920, ships carrying Russians who had fled the civil war were kept in quarantine off İstanbul before their passengers were allowed to land. Typhus was one of the main fears. Some later accounts say forty days, but contemporary memoirs and recent scholarship describe quarantines lasting from a few days to two weeks. I could not confirm forty days for the 1920 arrivals.23

A quarantine is rarely forty days now. It is ten days, or two weeks, or whatever the illness needs. The forty is still in the word.

The ship was held in quarantine.

Sources

  1. Etymologia: Quarantine — Emerging Infectious Diseases, CDC
  2. Mütareke Döneminde İstanbul’daki Rus Mültecilerin Yaşamı — Atatürk Araştırma Merkezi Dergisi XXII, 64–66 (2006)
  3. Constantinople/Istanbul as an Artistic Hub of the Émigrés from the former Russian Empire in 1919–1927 — Ekaterina Aygün, doctoral dissertation, LMU München (2024)

item.title: influence
item.description: Influence was once a fluid: medieval Latin influentia, a flowing in from the stars. Influenza is the same word, and flu is what is left of it.
item.content:encoded:
Influence means the power to affect someone or something. It comes from the medieval Latin influentia, a flowing in, from influere, to flow in.1

In the Middle Ages, influence was believed to be a fluid that streamed down from the stars into people and shaped their character and their fortune.1

Influenza is the same word. It is simply the Italian for influence, and epidemics were once blamed on the stars. Flu is what is left of it.1

He was under the influence.

Sources

  1. Influence — Merriam-Webster

item.title: bosh
item.description: Bosh, nonsense or empty talk, comes from the Turkish boş, meaning empty. It became current in English through J. J. Morier’s 1834 novel Ayesha, the Maid of Kars.
item.content:encoded:
Bosh means nonsense or empty talk in English. It comes from the Turkish word boş, meaning empty.1

It became current in English in the nineteenth century through J. J. Morier’s 1834 novel Ayesha, the Maid of Kars. What was empty in Turkish became empty talk in English, and then nonsense.12

It is old-fashioned now, but it is still there.

You’re talking bosh.
